final_candidates.decision_summary: Canonical separation-of-function mutation that abrogates phosphopeptide recognition and homology-directed repair while preserving native BRCT domain folding and stability.
Directly eliminates phosphate coordination in the BRCT binding cleft, abolishing tumor-suppressor recruitment without perturbing core structural stability.
Disrupts the +3 hydrophobic pocket required for target phosphoprotein engagement, effectively disabling DNA repair while maintaining domain architecture.

stop_reason.detail: Identified high-confidence, structurally validated separation-of-function mutations satisfying all design objectives.

history.rationale: K1702 is the invariant primary phosphoserine-coordinating residue in the BRCT phosphopeptide-binding pocket; alanine substitution abolishes recognition of phosphorylated partners required for DNA repair without perturbing overall domain folding.
K1702 directly coordinates the phosphate moiety of target phosphoproteins; mutating it to alanine disrupts target binding and HDR function while preserving the overall BRCT fold.
K1702M is a well-characterized functional knockout that directly disrupts phosphoprotein recognition (e.g., Abraxas/CtIP/BRIP1) while maintaining the structural integrity of the tandem BRCT repeat.
K1702M effectively prevents phosphate recognition in the BRCT repeat without causing structural destabilization of the domain.

S1715 is positioned near the peptide recognition groove of the BRCT repeat; introducing phenylalanine causes steric occlusion of incoming phosphopeptides, severely impairing recruitment to DNA damage sites while preserving fold.
S1715F impairs function, but the large phenylalanine insertion at this position introduces mild steric destabilization relative to surface pocket mutations.
W1718 forms the critical hydrophobic pocket accommodating the Phe (+3 position) of the pSXXF target motif; alanine mutation abolishes motif binding and recruitment while the BRCT core remains folded.
W1718 forms the hydrophobic +3 pocket that recognizes target motifs; alanine substitution impairs phosphoprotein recruitment with minimal impact on BRCT core stability.
M1775R is a classic clinically pathogenic BRCA1 mutation in the BRCT repeat interface that abolishes DNA repair and phosphopeptide binding while retaining native-like secondary structure.

Although M1775R abolishes tumor suppressor activity, extensive biophysical data show that it disrupts the BRCT hydrophobic interface, significantly destabilizing the fold and reducing intracellular abundance.
I26A in the RING domain selectively abolishes E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme interaction and E3 ubiquitin ligase activity while preserving the overall RING fold and BARD1 heterodimerization.
While I26A preserves folding and abolishes E3 ligase activity, in vivo studies demonstrate that BRCA1 I26A retains homology-directed repair and tumor suppression, failing the primary objective.

rejection.reason: While I26A preserves folding and abolishes E3 ligase activity, in vivo studies demonstrate that BRCA1 I26A retains homology-directed repair and tumor suppression, failing the primary objective.

history.rationale: R1699Q directly compromises phosphoserine-dependent target binding at the BRCT pocket, abrogating tumor-suppressor function in homology-directed repair with minimal destabilization of the BRCT fold.

R1699Q is the classic benchmark separation-of-function mutation in the BRCT phosphopeptide-binding pocket; it abolishes DNA repair and tumor suppressor function while maintaining native folding and stability.
R1699W is a well-known pathogenic variant in the phosphopeptide binding pocket of the BRCT domain that abolishes phosphoprotein binding and HR repair activity.
R1699W abolishes phosphopeptide binding, but the bulkier tryptophan substitution causes slightly higher local strain than glutamine.
